item.title: How do you get a job in M&A?
item.description:
M&A professionals work with clients on deals to buy and sell companies. M&A juniors put together pitchbooks in PowerPoint to help banks win a role advising on deals. M&A juniors also work on Excel models to help value the companies involved in deals. M&A jobs can be paid. A $110k salary in year one is considered typical. Bonuses for senior M&A bankers can reach seven figures. M&A jobs can involve gruelling hours. 100-hour weeks </news/2022/06/100-hour-weeks-banking> are not unheard of. Even just two years in M&A can leave you well positioned for the future. Opportunities for ex-M&A juniors are available in private equity, hedge funds, corporate finance, and elsewhere.
A job working in Mergers & Acquisitions (M&A) is one of the most sought-after and high-profile roles in investment banking </news/the-investment-banking-recruitment-process>. Senior M&A bankers travel the world and advise on the world’s biggest and most complex deals, reshaping entire industries.
M&A bankers are professional advisors. They operate at the highest levels, working with large global companies (“corporates”, as they’re known in banking), advising chief executives how best to position their organizations for the future.
Unlike management consultants, who help companies determine and implement the best strategy without necessarily changing the company’s component parts, M&A bankers drive strategy through structural change. They encourage the companies they’re working with (known as clients) to join together with other companies as equals (a merger), to buy and control a smaller company or part of a company (an acquisition), or to sell part of their own operations (a disposal).
Mergers, acquisitions, and disposals happen for different strategic reasons. For example, a client may decide to merge with a rival operating in the same business area to increase its market share. This is known as a horizontal merger.
Alternatively, a client may decide to acquire one of the companies that supplies the components necessary to fabricate its product. This is a vertical merger. There are also conglomerate mergers, when a company merges with or acquires a firm operating in a totally different market. And there are congeneric mergers, which take place when companies are in the same industry but offer different products. Conglomerate mergers have the advantage of allowing clients to enter completely different markets. Congeneric mergers bring advantages like established distribution channels, or whole new product lines.
Globally, the top three banks in M&A are Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and JPMorgan, as shown in the table below. These are the banks that work on the biggest and the most complex deals, often involving buyers and sellers in different countries. But there are a number of other big U.S. and European banks that are also active in M&A, and many also lend the money to finance the deals.
While the biggest, multi-billion-dollar deals like Paramount's $111bn acquisition of Warner Bros grab the headlines, the majority of deals are below $500m in size, and there are a number of so-called mid-market M&A firms which earn good money advising on these deals. There is also a large number of so-called boutique investment banks </news/2023/01/boutique-investment-banks>, which are often independent, privately-owned firms run by a small number of senior M&A bankers who’ve left big banks to set up on their own.
Boutiques are typically pure advisory houses – unlike banks, they don’t provide the financing for deals themselves. Some of the largest boutiques are publicly listed. The best-known boutiques include Evercore, Lazard, Rothschild, Moelis, Centerview Partners, PJT Partners, and Perella Weinberg Partners.
The top M&A bankers are known as “rainmakers” for their ability to land big deals, but beneath the glamour the hours are long. Junior bankers have to spend years learning their trade before they can generate their own deals.
What does an M&A analyst actually do?
Read More: What does an M&A analyst actually do? </news/what-are-ma-jobs>
M&A analysts are the lowest rung in the banking hierarchy </news/finance/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds-really>. Working as an analyst in an M&A division means being flexible, because you are often working on multiple projects at any point in time. You will be working on both live deals and pitching new ones. When you’re working on a live deal, you’ll be involved in deal execution or helping a client buy or sell an asset, respectively called buy-side or sell-side mandates. When you’re pitching, you’ll be preparing documents, PowerPoint presentations specifically, for senior bankers to use as they persuade clients to do new deals.
Typically, an M&A analyst will also be responsible for the financial analysis that underpins an M&A deal. This includes building a financial model, running the valuation and financial impact analysis, and preparing materials to present this analysis to the client. Sometimes they will also be the point of contact for any questions or requests from the client relating to the analysis, but analysts are rarely placed in front of clients.
“Day-to-day life as an M&A </news/what-s-it-really-like-to-work-in-m-and-a-a-day-in-the-life-of-a-junior-m-and-a-banker> analyst largely depends on the deals you are working on,” says the head of UK M&A at one European bank. “Broadly speaking, mornings and early afternoons involve client interaction, status and/or diligence calls and discussions to agree on the workstreams the deal team should focus on as well as next steps. By the afternoon or evening, meetings are less frequent, and you can focus on progressing on the deliverables, which can range from excel models to the preparation of marketing materials [pitchbooks].”
What are hours like in an M&A job?
They are tough. When deals boomed after the COVID pandemic, some junior bankers at Goldman Sachs complained that they were working </news/2021/03/goldman-sachs-analyst-survey-working-hours> more than 100 hours a week and that they were on the verge of collapse. M&A analysts at other banks voiced similar complaints and the banking industry responded by increasing junior bankers’ salaries and making sure juniors get some time off at weekends.
In 2026, however, long hours are still common </news/finance-best-lifestyle>. 75 hours a week are not unusual at big banks – especially American ones – and boutiques can regularly reach 85-hour work weeks on average.
Our Compensation & Lifestyle Reports </banking-compensation-guide>, which compiled average working hours for M&A professionals, found that the average M&A banker worked 67.1 hours a week on average in 2023, 67.9 hours a week in 2024, and 67.3 hours a week on average in 2025.
The death of Jefferies associate Carter McIntosh </news/jefferies-associate-died> in May last year was suspected at the time of being due to "pulling crazy hours", but a later investigation showed it was a fatal combination of cocaine and fentanyl </news/carter-mcintosh-jefferies>. The long work hours mean that drugs are rife in investment banking - Adderall is a popular choice </news/bankers-adderall> of stimulant.
Junior M&A bankers work so hard because M&A is a fast-paced job, and juniors will often work on multiple deals. Deal execution tends to be unpredictable by nature: it’s a live situation and a client-driven activity.
The work of pitching clients who might participate in M&A deals tends to be more predictable, but senior bankers will often ask juniors to make changes to the PowerPoint presentations advertising the deal late at night – the famous “pls fix” email. But the hours aren't always extreme; “working full weekends and very late nights may occasionally happen around a particular deal, but these hours are not the norm,” says the M&A head.
There are upsides. One Morgan Stanley banker tells us that “M&A analysts have the opportunity to manage their own time, and as long as the work gets delivered to a high standard, you have the freedom to fit the job around your personal commitments.”
What is your career path in M&A?
One of the benefits of a career in M&A is that there is regular and steady progression, and a clear promotion path </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds>. You start as an analyst, become an associate after a few years, a vice president (VP) a few years after that, a director a few years after that, and then a managing director (MD) if you qualify. The exact titles can vary between different banks </news/finance/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds-really>.
“Meritocracy is key to this path,” says Joe Hannon, head of UK mergers & acquisitions for UBS. The time it takes to reach the top rung varies, but as a (very rough) rule of thumb, it’s around 10 years – if you get there at all, as the skillsets needed for a junior and senior banker are very different.
That’s if you decide to stay in banking – but M&A jobs offer a wide variety of exit options. Many graduates stay at banks for their two-year M&A analyst training program, and then leave for jobs in private equity, management consulting, and corporate development teams in large companies, among others.
M&A analysts are in very high demand. They are frequently poached by rival firms and rival industries, such as private equity: a talent war that reached a crescendo in the summer of 2024, in which private equity firms were recruiting bank juniors before they even started their jobs, led JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon to call the practice “unethical”. They put a pause on it for around six months, and according to recruiter Anthony Keizner of Odyssey Search Partners in Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/private-equity-firm-on-cycle-recruiting-return-after-pause-2026-1>, are actually more satisfied with their slightly-more-experienced banking analysts.
Banks, however, are going to some length to prevent their juniors from leaving for private equity. JPMorgan </news/jp-morgan-bankers-leave-for-private-equity>, for example, told its analysts last year that they are immediately obliged to disclose if they have accepted a job offer elsewhere. In return for honesty, the bank will fire anyone who accepts an offer elsewhere. Goldman Sachs, also recently, now requires analysts to swear an oath </news/goldman-sachs-oath> every three months that they haven’t accepted a job elsewhere.

The latter becomes more important over the years. item.title: Bad luck to all the bankers who thought private credit jobs would make them rich
item.description:
Once upon a time, private credit pay was rising. Today, this is no longer the case.
When Blackstone published its second quarter results a few weeks ago, "realized performance compensation" (carried interest) </news/what-is-carried-interest>it paid to employees in its private credit and insurance segment was down 51% year-on-year in the first half.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Blackstone is not alone in crimping private credit pay. The latest report from Wall Street compensation consultancy Johnson Associates, predicts performance compensation in private credit firms will be flat to down 10% this year. That's both better and worse than in May, when Johnson was predicting that private credit performance pay would be down between 2.5% and 7.5%. Johnson Associates' predictions are based on detailed interviews with people in the market.
While people working in private credit are probably having their pay squeezed, people working in public debt markets are probably having their pay inflated. Johnson Associates thinks bonuses for debt capital markets </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm> (DCM) professionals in investment banks will increase by 5% to 10% this year. This less than the 20% to 30% bonus hikes Johnson Associates is predicting for equity capital markets bankers and equities markets, but it is an increase at least.
The increase is worth noting because it wasn't so long ago that DCM bankers </news/dcm-bankers-in-2025> were leaving banks to work for private credit firms. In early 2025, Macquarie even closed its 80 person </news/the-apollo-chart-suggesting-private-credit-is-eating-banking-jobs>US DCM team. In the years after the pandemic, private credit was a very sexy place to work. </news/private-credit-jobs>In the middle of 2025, Goldman Sachs even began distributing carried interest-type payments to its senior bankers to stop them from leaving. <https://www.wsj.com/articles/goldman-takes-the-lead-in-carry-pay-for-bankers-b2fa5841>
There's no need for that now. Private credit is not the source of riches it once seemed. Ares, the private capital firm which has 66% of its $671bn of assets invested in private credit, is swiftly diversifying into private equity. <https://www.ft.com/content/9f446812-5dc9-4d25-9a4b-ac5162e62d81?syn-25a6b1a6=1>Blue Owl shares are still down over 50% from their 2025 peak.
To the extent that there's a moral in the story, it's that you should not chase shiny jobs. Debt capital markets (DCM) bankers are in fashion; private credit people are not. Speaking to us earlier this year, Johnson Associates' figurehead Alan Johnson said private credit professionals will need to adjust to their new pay reality. "They thought it would go to the sky," he reflected. Instead it's falling back to earth, and doing so harder with each passing quarter.

item.title: Citadel Securities hired a semiconductor architect and Goldman Sachs MD
item.description:
Semiconductor stocks may have hit a rough patch </news/citadel-leopold-aschenbrenner-situational-awareness>last month, but the talent working on that technology is as in-demand as ever. Electronic market maker </news/high-frequency-trading-hiring-and-pay> Citadel Securities </news/day-in-the-life-trader-citadel-securities> recently hired the former CTO of a smaller semiconductor design firm, who was most recently plying his trade at Goldman Sachs. </news/how-to-get-a-job-goldman-sachs>
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Mayan Moudgill joined Citadel Securities last month in New York as a senior software engineer. He spent the last quarter century working across Goldman Sachs and Sandbridge Technologies, a semiconductor manufacturing firm. He spent the last five years at Goldman Sachs, where he was an MD within the bank's engineering division, but spent seven years before that as chief architect and CTO of Sandbridge. Moudgill was part of the Sandbridge founding team in 2001, and became a tech fellow at Goldman Sachs during his first stint there.
Moudgill is also credited on over 100 patent filings <https://patents.justia.com/inventor/mayan-moudgill> dating back to 1996. Many of these involve multithreading, where different threads of a program can run concurrently on different cores of a piece of hardware, allowing for significantly faster data analysis. His later patents, filed during his time at Sandbridge (which had changed names to Optimum Semiconductor Technologies after being acquired by a Chinese technology firm), were for a "neural network accellerator. <https://patents.justia.com/patent/12165030>"
Although Moudgill is joining as a software engineer, it seems likely that he will be working on hardware in some capacity. Citadel Securities declined to comment further than verifying his job title. It has a robust hardware engineering team which primarily works on Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs). </news/fpga-engineer-internships-and-graduate-jobs> It offers base salaries of up to $350k for FPGA engineers in current open job listings.

item.title: Point72 hired a discretionary macro trading head from a quant hedge fund
item.description:
AQR Capital Management </news/quant-hedge-fund-cio-we-stole-a-fair-bit-of-our-culture-from-goldman-sachs> is one of the biggest players in the quant hedge fund space, but it's not purely a quant fund. </news/biggest-quant-hedge-funds> It's home to several senior discretionary traders, one of whom has just defected to Point72 after 11 years at the fund.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Vinod Addidam joined Point72 this month as its global head of macro trading strategy. </news/2021/05/how-to-get-a-job-in-a-global-macro-fund> He reports to Mo Grimeh, the fund's global head of macro who joined from Millennium six years ago. Addidam will be working out of the fund's Stamford, Connecticut office, having already bought a house in the area last summer.
At AQR, Addidam was global head of equities and commodities trading, according to a biography <https://www.rblt.com/gelc-biography/vinod-addidam> from a Rosenblatt conference in 2022. The biography stated that he was "also responsible for the firm’s Capital Markets and AQR Arbitrage trading efforts." Before joining AQR, Addidam spent seven years at Deutsche Bank. He joined as an MBA associate and rose to director, serving as head of emerging markets delta one and arbitrage trading.
AQR seems to take a 'quantamental' approach to its macro trading business. An opening in its discretionary portfolio management division says that the team "works with the firm’s systematic researchers to jointly manage macro portfolios and the firm’s flagship Global Macro Strategy." Point72's global macro team specifies <https://point72.com/what-we-do/#:~:text=Point72%20Global%20Macro,LEARN%20MORE> that it makes discretionary investments first and foremost. It also has a systematic macro business which operates via the fund's quant arm Cubist Systematic Strategies.

item.title: A Singapore hedge fund that wants its 22-year-olds to be rich & happy is beating the rest
item.description:
One of the best performing hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> of 2026 so far is in Singapore. It is not comprised of seasoned portfolio managers </news/finance/portfolio-manager-job-hedge-fund-lifestyle> who have done their time in banks or rival funds. It does not churn through staff and ruthlessly eject poor performers. It likes to be kind. And it likes to hire people in their early 20s.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The fund is Quantedge, a systematic hedge fund based in Singapore which has been running for 20 years and has $6bn in assets under management. Figures released today from Bloomberg <https://x.com/nishantkumar07/status/2084908358373355933?s=20>say that its year-to-date returns are 34.6%. This compares to 8.2% at Millennium, 10.9% at Point72 and 12% at Citadel - after Citadel helpfully bought </news/citadel-leopold-aschenbrenner-situational-awareness> Leopold Aschenbrenner's </news/leopold-aschenbrenner-hedge-fund-24> publicly traded portfolio at a 10% discount.
Speaking on the Odds on Open podcast <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3LFV27B3A-U&t=4s> last week, Quantedge CEO Suhaimi Zainul-Abidin said the fund doesn't really hire "mid-career" or experienced portfolio managers. "We hire almost exclusively fresh out of school," he explained. There's a big intern class. This year's interns come from the likes of Nanyang Technological University, the London School of Economics and Yale.
While rival funds have a reputation for churning through humans, Zainul-Abidin said Quantedge hires people for the long term. The fund feels an obligation to "take care of this individual, to give them a job, a career that could last a lifetime," he declared. Quantedge wants its young employees to "grow individually" and "to be happy, to be taken care of." It wants them to "live a good life, build a family and so on." Hiring someone is a "huge responsibility," says Zainul-Abidin.
This all sounds very unlike big multistrategy hedge funds, which often hire experienced portfolio managers from rivals for huge sums of money and let them go when risk limits are exceeded. But Quantedge is clearly doing something right. Not only has it returned 34.6% this year, but it's also returned nearly 20% on average every year since inception. The intention has been to create a compounding engine, says Zainul-Abidin.
Quantedge's successful strategy is to "operate one of the most diversified investment portfolios in the world." It trades 300 distinct markets and 50 different commodity types and it researches each of them. In these areas it takes a higher than usual level of risk. "When you have a, "diversified portfolio your idiosyncratic risk goes down tremendously," explains Zainul-Abidin. More risk can therefore be taken in each individual investment.
This works for Quantedge. It also works for the 22-year-olds it likes to hire. After they've worked there for a while they get to invest in Quantedge's fund and to enjoy some compounding of their own, although only 10% of their money can be withdrawn each year.
If you're a 22-year-old looking for a benevolent protector, this all sounds very wonderful. Although it's a quant fund, Quantedge doesn't only hire mathematicians. Zainul-Abidin himself has a legal background. "You can be in any field," he says. "You can be an engineer. You can be a computer scientist." It's about being able to think logically and systematically.
Zainul-Abidin says Quantedge is not into "being maniacally meritocratic." Nor is it into dumping its people after a loss. "Just because you're not profitable for one, two years doesn't mean that it [your strategy] can't be the part of the portfolio that saves it [the fund] in two or three years' time," he declares.
If this sounds appealing, Quantedge is also into hiring smart polymaths who want to 'get on board' with its mission and who will think collectively. Quantedge's mission is to make its mostly private investors and employees very rich. Thinking collectively means understanding the big Quantedge picture and not being too hung up on your own personal performance.
If you're still not convinced, Quantedge also has a Formula One simulator in an office. It has offices in Singapore and New York. In salary terms it pays well, but maybe not the best. <https://wwwdontmesswith6a.blogspot.com/2022/07/singapore-tech-internshipfresh-graduate.html>Mostly it is about being nice, and making you rich in the long term. "If you're having any trouble elsewhere, let us know. We'll try to help you because you're now part of the Quantedge family," says Zainul-Abidin of his ethos towards his young employees.

item.title: How AI is changing careers in M&A
item.description:
People working in M&A </news/what-are-ma-jobs> work very, very long hours </news/finance-best-lifestyle>. Many of those hours – especially for junior professionals – are not spent doing anything particularly interesting. But that might change in the future, as there is a monster on the hill – AI.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
The impact of AI on M&A specifically might be one of the most discussed in the industry. But discussions are often vague. Paul Uren, JPMorgan’s head of investment banking in APAC, made some utterances on the benefits to Reuters <https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/jpmorgan-rolls-out-ai-tools-investment-banking-globally-senior-banker-says-2026-05-21/> earlier this year. “We are in the early phase adopting AI tools throughout our investment banking business globally but are excited by the developments,” Uren explained. “We're finding ⁠that AI streamlines the preparation of content and materials, as well as helping bankers engage with more clients more efficiently.”
“Content and materials” means pitchbooks and models. Pitchbooks are the big PowerPoint presentations that banks use to pitch to new companies. Models refers to the vast spreadsheets that banks use to value a business and what impact a merger would have on its accounts.
AI firms have noticed that there's an opportunity here. Anthropic has a head of financial services product, former Morgan Stanley banker Nicholas Lin </news/junior-bankers-ai-jobs>. Anthropic has already announced ten “agent templates” for financial services professionals, including pitchbooks, monitoring earnings reviews, and building financial models.
OpenAI is not too far behind <http://efinancialcareers.com/news/openai-job-banker>; it has more than 100 ex-investment bankers helping to train its models to build financial models. They were being paid around $150 an hour after careers at JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, and Goldman Sachs, Bloomberg reported <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-10-21/openai-looks-to-replace-the-drudgery-of-junior-bankers-workload?srnd=homepage-americas> last year.
AI, by building models and pitchbooks, can do what a banker does, but much quicker, and really much cheaper. Bain & Company, the consulting firm, noted <https://www.bain.com/about/media-center/press-releases/2026/global-ma-momentum-builds-in-2026-as-megadeals-surge-but-acquirers-confront-a-new-ai-winners-paradoxbain-company-ma-midyear-report/> that AI can analyse “procurement contracts, supply chain networks, R&D portfolios, and charts of accounts to confirm cost-synergy opportunities” two to three times faster than a human being can.
Sumeet Chabria, a former Bank of America executive who now runs consultancy ThoughtLinks, informed Business Insider last year <https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-shape-4-investment-banking-careers-ecm-dcm-advisory-trading-2025-8> that 30% of M&A processes could be automated by AI by 2030, and that this automation will include scanning public & private financial data and flagging operational, market, and geopolitical risks. Flesh-and-blood bankers will still review risks, provide context, and take the lead on “final” due diligence, though. Actual humans will also shape deal strategy and advise clients.
The consequence of further adoption will be job cuts. Debasish Patnaik, head of McKinsey’s AI consulting arm QuantumBlack, told Fortune <https://fortune.com/2026/06/07/banks-mass-workforce-cuts-ai-entry-level-jobs-junior-analysts/> in June that junior analyst classes would be cut by as much as two thirds due to AI.
Banks are unlikely to cut analyst/intern classes altogether, however. “Banking is an apprenticeship business. Today’s junior analysts become tomorrow’s managing directors,” Patnaik told Fortune. “Senior judgment cannot be manufactured laterally.”
Some banks are already trying to engineer a replacement for the apprenticeship. Lawrence Shaw, Deutsche Bank's head of workforce capability, thinks the answer </news/deutsche-bank-juniors-imaginary-clients> is to push analysts and associates in front of clients earlier with more training. The training will involve fake deals using virtual, AI clients.
Jobs in M&A will become harder to find in the meantime. Jobs are harder to come by </news/banking-jobs-2026>. Banks are talking less about investing in people, and more about investing in AI – Citi CFO Gonzalo Luchetti, for example, said in the firm’s Q1 of 2026 analyst call that AI could “turbocharge” its investments, and that it intended to end the year with less headcount than it started it.
Lazard’s </news/lazard-md-spending> workforce might be the canary in the coalmine; the firm currently has a ratio of around 1:6 of dealmakers to junior bankers, and says it wants fewer juniors. It’s been suggested that that number might come down to 1:3, or perhaps even less.
Something unlikely to change in the industry is the number of hours worked, unfortunately. An M&A banker told us </news/ai-is-not-going-to-get-rid-of-18-hour-days-for-investment-bank-analysts> back in February that, even though many parts of investment banking would become automated, the 18-hour workdays will still stick around. Managing directors will still expect meetings to be scheduled and to happen. If they happen quicker, then all the best – book more meetings. “Hours will get slightly better, but not dramatically. I just don't see a world where analysts will uniformly finish at 8pm,” he said.
Much of the above is still theory. In practice, AI might even be able to advise on an entire deal from start to finish: the Wall Street Journal reported <https://www.wsj.com/pro/private-equity/ai-replaced-bankers-on-a-cvc-sale-process-ce9b765b?utm> earlier this year that €200bn private equity firm CVC Capital Partners used AI to sell a Greek e-commerce business for €635m. The WSJ reported that prospective buyers were welcomed to talk to a chatbot versed on the deal, answering questions on financials and due diligence.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Junior Deutsche bankers will be given imaginary clients. The world’s most profitable hedge fund is in Japan
item.description:
There’s a certain amount of angst about the effect of AI on financial sector employment. Some people think that bankers are “the new coal miners <https://x.com/alexanderrX_/status/2084355821991854423>” while others think AI offers a great opportunity <https://www.ft.com/content/b1fce826-d286-41b9-9823-e767f09df999> to get close to the client instead of building Excel models and changing fonts on PowerPoint presentations. Everyone seems to agree that the problem is to find a way of incorporating AI into the workflow without disrupting the process by which human capital is built. Or to put it another way, if the AI is able to do all the work of compiling decks, building models and responding to “pls fix” requests, how will young bankers learn their trade?
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Lawrence Shaw, the head of workforce capability at Deutsche Bank <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/hsbc-signals-bonus-hike-as-revenue-jumps-c73e832d>, believes he has the solution. Shaw says the answer is that the juniors can start off by using their real intelligence on artificial clients. Shaw says the job of a junior banker will have to change so that analysts and associates </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> get into client-facing roles at an earlier stage, and that they will need to be trained in “how to take information out of the model and use it with the client”.
Because nobody in their right mind is going to let a recent graduate say much in meetings on a multi-million dollar transaction, this training will involve a certain amount of simulation. Shaw says that “we’re looking at using avatar client interactions for our junior staff” (as well as making more of an effort to take them along to meet real clients, on a supervised basis).
It’s not completely clear what this “avatar” will be – a full-scale ABBA Voyage <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABBA_Voyage>-style hologram might be a bit overkill, but it might be a bit disappointing if all it means is the same chatbot, made up to look like a Bloomberg chat. Possibly it will be somewhere in between; something that can simulate a video call, but which can’t be mistaken for anything you might invite to lunch.
Although it sounds science fictional, pilots have been training in simulators for ages, and many banks have used “war games” and pretend exercises as part of their process. Adding AI into the mix just potentially makes the whole thing more realistic, and therefore better.
However, the trouble with simulator training (as anyone can tell you if they have tried to transfer paper-trading results to real money) is that a digital avatar differs from a real client precisely in the fact that you know they are just pretend. If they get mad at you, it doesn’t really matter; if you lose them a ton of money, it doesn’t have any real effect on the bank. It is a lot easier to develop good habits of clear thinking in this sort of situation, but there is a huge risk that all those habits suddenly desert you the first time you’re put under the stress of having high stakes.
Elsewhere, there is a multi-strategy trading shop </news/multistrategy-hedge-funds-hiring>out there which has been actively trading forex and short term interest rates way back since the 1990s. Although it doesn’t publish audited results, its cumulative P&L in FX alone is about $345bn. And when combined with rates, equities and other smaller strategies, its returns are credibly estimated to have been well above $200bn per year, every year for the last decade.
This enviable performance has been achieved, of course, by the General Account of the Ministry of Finance of Japan <https://www.ft.com/content/7ff5dd5c-dc45-4db3-ab75-8ab1c844f7be>. The overall benefit to Japan of its well-timed interventions in the markets has been of the order of 6% of GDP, an extremely useful boost to an otherwise quite tight fiscal position. So why aren’t pod shops rushing to poach its traders and reserves managers?
We would suggest that this is mostly because it's significantly easier to trade macro when you’re working for the entity that makes the big macro decisions. If any other hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> were to trade on the basis of confidential information about central bank and finance ministry policy, the regulators would probably get involved. The most profitable trading desk in Asia is, unfortunately, the clearest example possible of the truism that often, people can look like market wizards, but all the value is in the franchise of the seat that they occupy.
Meanwhile …
Apparently, all the cute viral videos that Blackstone’s Jon Gray puts out (including his jogging series) are reviewed by compliance first, just in case. He notes that this means it’s easier for him to be a social media star than it is for junior bankers. (Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/jon-gray-running-video-viral-blackstone-intern-analyst-2026-7>)
Two medium-sized ponds get new big fish, as Bank of America promotes Simbah Mustasa and Sjoerd van Hooijdonk to be heads of investment banking in Africa and Benelux respectively. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-04/bank-of-america-taps-new-africa-benelux-investment-bank-leads>)
The massive Goldman Sachs office in Dallas is still being built, and Aasem Khalil, the partner in charge of it, is trying to get the nickname “Y’all Street” to stick. (NPR <https://www.npr.org/2026/08/04/nx-s1-5697067/texas-banking-goldman-sachs-wall-street>)
Dymon Asia appears to be trying to break into the big leagues of multi-strategy. After a number of top level hires in London, it has now recruited Jay Radia, a former Goldman Sachs employee who was most recently chief operating officer of BlueCrest’s commodities business. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/dymon-asia-hires-bluecrests-jay-radia-in-commodities-push-3a5b1793>)
“Tax loss harvesting” is the technique of optimising your trading strategy so that temporary fluctuations get turned into tax credits, allowing you to declare potentially millions in losses on a portfolio that’s trebled. It’s been industrialised as a process by Cliff Asness and AQR, to the extent that some people are worrying that the loophole will be closed. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/features/2026-aqr-tax-loss-harvesting-billionaires/>)
For some reason, the rise of Ozempic has made a lot of people lose all sense of what kind of questions it might be appropriate to ask their colleagues. (Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/ozempic-weight-loss-drugs-causing-awkward-work-conversations-hr-nightmares-2026-8>)
One of the great things about Australian financial media is that things like “controversy and disagreement over two executives’ job moves” get described as a “stoush”. (AFR <https://www.afr.com/companies/financial-services/jarden-probes-bankers-relationship-amid-barrenjoey-defection-stoush-20260730-p60k4z>)

item.title: A Citadel quant developer joined Kalshi and declared himself very excited
item.description:
As we reported last week </news/traders-earning-1m-on-kalshi-are-offered-double-or-nothing-to-join-trading-firms>, some quants appear to be earning $1m+ placing trades on Kalshi and everyone wants to hire them. But what if you're a quant working for Kalshi itself? Then you might have to tolerate a salary of $150k+, plus equity. This is also exciting, given that the prediction markets firm is contemplating an IPO <https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/24/kalshi-ceo-says-company-thinking-about-ipo-but-not-for-this-year-.html> in late 2027 or 2028.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Chao Peng, a New York based quantitative developer who's spent the past six years at hedge fund Citadel has joined Kalshi and has declared himself "excited" about the fact on LinkedIn. Nearly 550 people have liked his post. Many of them also seem to work for Citadel, or in financial services. Presumably they would be excited to join Kalshi too.
It's not just the fact that Kalshi offers an opportunity to gain stock in what might be next year's big IPO (which Peng doesn't actually mention), but that Kalshi is still new. It was launched in 2021, whereas Citadel has been about since 1990. Kalshi is so new that, "Most of what makes those markets work is still being built, and now I get to build it," says Peng. Kalshi only launched the ability to trades perpetual future contracts <https://news.kalshi.com/p/kalshi-launches-perpetual-futures-america> on the platform in late May, for example. Perp trading crossed a billion in volume <https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/09/kalshi-perpetual-futures-trading-perps-crosses-1-billion-in-volume-within-a-week-of-launch.html> within a week of being launched.
If Peng feels excited about working for Kalshi, other financial services quants will probably feel similar. Peng has spent his entire career working on trading platforms, first at Beacon and then at Citadel and has a Masters in Financial Engineering from Baruch. </news/baruch-mfe-course>
Kalshi is upping its game. In May it hired Sudhir Jain, a former derivatives regulator and JPMorgan executive director. It's just launched "Kalshi pro" for people "who want to trade many markets at once with speed and precision." It clearly has plans. Quant developers may want to pay attention.

item.title: "My bank cut jobs last Wednesday. My manager was thoughtlessly malicious"
item.description:
This time last week, the bank I work for cut jobs. I was not among the people cut, but a few people I know were. It was a difficult day for them and the thoughtless behaviour of our manager made it far worse.
The team I work for was set up a few years ago. It was founded in 2021 and many of us joined at that time. However, several senior people left in 2023-2024. At that point, the team over-hired massively in response.
Last week's cuts were intended to remedy the over-hiring. Deal-flow in our area is down and the front office team we support has built its own bench and automated several tasks. We're not really needed and none of us was really that surprised when people were let go. In some areas, 20% of people were cut.
What was surprising was the behaviour of the manager. After cutting the team, he left for a company event in the evening. Most of us didn't attend this event but someone there helpfully took photos of the happy times.
Plenty of the people who were fired on Wednesday were asked to continue working through to Friday. On Thursday, the manager's assistant circulated the photos of him the previous evening. He was drinking, playing games and generally having a great time.
It seemed very insensitive. People who had just been told their jobs were disappearing were expected to celebrate their manager having a night out, fully paid for for by the bank. Many of them felt like they were having salt rubbed in their wounds. I know several who wanted to leave immediately but who couldn't because they didn't want to jeopardise their severance payments.
The whole thing seems incomprehensibly insensitive. Morale was already low and is now even lower. Everyone on the team is extremely hard working and has been well respected in the bank. The thoughtless managers on the team have been the real issue. The events of the last week have simply confirmed that.
Michael Cormick is a pseudonym

item.title: What qualifications and skills do you need for a career in electronic trading
item.description:
In top electronic trading firms </news/high-frequency-trading-hiring-and-pay>, there's a notion that the specifics of your education don't matter. Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street>, for example, says that it's "more interested in how you think and learn than what you currently know," and doesn't expect applicants to know much about finance. Despite this, the profile of most students going into electronic trading is remarkably similar.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
When we assessed Jane Street's intern </news/high-frequency-trading-internship> class last year, </news/this-is-what-it-takes-to-get-a-64k-jane-street-internship> we found that most of its successful applicants studied mathematics, computer science, or a mix of both. Traders </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> and researchers </news/what-is-a-quant-researcher-hedge-fund> were more likely to be mathematicians while computer scientists went into engineering roles.
Successful applicants usually attend top schools. </news/2013/07/the-best-universities-for-jobs-in-trading-ma-and-risk> Schools like MIT and Harvard provide a lot of entry level hires to Jane Street </news/jane-street-target-universities> and Citadel Securities </news/the-universities-that-will-get-you-a-300k-job-at-citadel-securities>. In Europe, Oxbridge, the French Grandes Ecoles </news/2023/02/best-grande-ecole-finance> and Russian technology institutes </news/best-university-for-quant-finance-career>are prestigious. In Asia, the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) </news/the-elite-graduates-earning-insane-salaries-in-electronic-trading> are a key source of talent.
Even if you attend one of these schools, you're not guaranteed of a place. You'll need top grades, but you'll also need something more. Quant </news/quant-jobs-finance>careers coach Ash Cross told us in February </news/put-your-questions-to-the-coach-who-can-get-you-a-job-in-electronic-trading>that "a lot of US students with a 4.0 score in their undergraduate degrees don't have internships." No internship </news/highest-paying-internships-finance> usually means no graduate job.
If you're early in your studies, there are plenty of things you can do. Apply for all the spring weeks, insight events and trading competitions </news/how-important-are-spring-weeks-and-insight-events-when-applying-for-quant-trading-internships> that electronic trading firms run. They have low acceptance rates, around 1%, but some internships in the space are even more selective, accepting as little as 0.1% of applicants.
If you're at the end of your undergraduate studies, you're in a bit more of a pickle. You can go into further education but, counterintuitively, spending more time in education might hurt your chances. James Holland, director of recruitment firm Quant Capital, previously told us </news/prop-trading-firms-won-t-touch-ph-d-quants-try-banking-instead> that prop trading </news/prop-trading-workplace-culture-inappropriate-flirting-bullying> firms sometimes discriminate against PhDs </news/do-you-need-a-phd-for-a-quant-job-in-finance>when hiring because "they find those people too academic, too stubborn, and too set in their ways." PhDs are, comparatively, loved much more in banks </news/algo-trader-banking-vs-trading-firms> and hedge funds. </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>
Trading firms make exceptions for PhDs who have studied more niche or theoretical topics. You might need a PhD in electronic engineering to work on hardware like ASICs, FPGAs </news/fpga-engineer-internships-and-graduate-jobs> or GPUs </news/programming-languages-machine-learning-ai-quant>in a trading firm. Jane Street previously stated </news/jane-street-employees-reveal-what-degrees-matter-when-applying-for-quant-jobs> that the majority of its researchers aren't PhDs, but its PhD headcount had grown to 160 </news/does-jane-street-hire-phds> as of March. Petter Kolm, head of NYU Courant's mathematics in finance program, said that "postgraduate training will still be valuable, especially for research-heavy roles."
If you don't want to risk committing yourself to education for an extra 5+ years, you could try a masters. Master in financial engineering (MFE) courses </news/top-masters-in-financial-engineering-courses>are popular for giving students a chance to learn about finance before jumping into a quant job </news/quant-jobs-are-some-of-the-hardest-in-finance-but-they-re-getting-even-harder>, and they're known for having strong recruitment pipelines. Top courses are hard to get into, however, and many of the lower ranked MFE courses are substandard </news/masters-in-finance-worth-it> for a career in an electronic trading firm. The gold standard is Baruch College in New York, which is both cost effective and offers access to the highest paying jobs. Baruch students earn as much as $25k per month as interns at trading firms like Tower Research Capital as well as hedge funds like Point72. Getting onto the Baruch course requires being able to answer questions like 'in how many ways can you make a bracelet with ten different beads?' </news/baruch-mfe-course> Princeton and Carnegie Mellon also offer some of the MFE courses in America.
If you really want to stand out, you'll need to impress much earlier in your education. Electronic trading </news/best-electronic-trading-for-to-work-for> alums have said that these firms begin recruiting at high school and have particularly strong presences in Olympiad tournaments </news/networking-for-1m-quant-and-ai-jobs-really-begins-at-14-years-old> for subjects like mathematics and informatics.
Return to our guide to electronic trading here. </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>

item.title: Millennium's head of equities trading technology has left after two years
item.description:
Working for a major hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> can often mean sitting out of the market for years at a time on lengthy non-competes. Rick Lane, a technologist, spent 15 months on the sidelines before joining Millennium </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-hedge-fund-millennium> in 2024; two years later he's tending to the garden once more.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Lane worked as Millennium's head of equities trading technology. He joined from rival hedge fund Citadel, </news/2022/10/how-to-get-a-job-at-citadel>where he worked in its core technology business which focuses on technology for its risk and trading businesses. He left that role in the summer of 2023 before sitting out that 15-month noncompete.
It's not clear where Lane will go after finishing his current gardening leave period. He did not respond to a request for comment.
It's understood that, rather than appointing a replacement, Millennium will distribute Lane's duties among existing employees. Current openings in the trading technology team are limited; there's one open listing for a junior/mid-level engineer in Singapore.
Millennium declined to comment.

item.title: A French ED cut by Morgan Stanley in London is safe at Deutsche Bank in New York
item.description:
Mark Vaillant has got a new job. Good for him. He was last working for Morgan Stanley in London for nearly five years after joining from Goldman Sachs, but then Morgan Stanley reportedly cut him <https://www.risk.net/people/7963318/people-citadel-and-brevan-snag-banks%E2%80%99-top-traders-and-more>along with four other people on the FX real money sales desk in March.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Now Vaillant is back. He is not at Morgan Stanley. He is not in London. He is at Deutsche Bank in New York.
Vaillant didn't respond to a request to comment on what he is doing at Deutsche Bank, but he has written on LinkedIn that he is head of EM macro sales into US real money and hedge fund clients there.
This appears to be a superior job to his last one as an executive director (ED) working on 'emerging market FX and rates sales for real money and hedge fund clients' at Morgan Stanley.
Good things can clearly come of losing your job. Vaillant isn't even American. He is French. Deutsche Bank is building its US macro team and isn't set on hiring Americans. The head of US rates trading there is Pedro Goldbaum, </news/pedro-goldbaum-deutsche-bank>who is Brazilian and was at Citi in London before he arrived in 2024.
Also let go from Morgan Stanley with Vaillant were Nayab Khan, Tyler Hambleton and Georgina Hingley. Khan is now at RBC and Hingley is at Natixis. We don't know about Hambleton, Maybe he should approach Deutsche Bank in New York too?

item.title: The skills you need for a career in M&A
item.description:
A career in M&A </news/what-are-ma-jobs> is appealing to just about everyone. High pay, high prestige, excellent exit opportunities – it’s not a hard sell. But is a career in M&A for everyone? What skillset do you need to thrive?
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
You’ll need to be able to work autonomously. “M&A analysts are expected to get up the curve in terms of financial analysis and technical skills in a short period of time, and the role also requires a degree of independent and proactive work (for example reading broker notes) to stay current on the market environment,” a member of the global M&A team at Morgan Stanley told us four years ago. That was a while ago; AI can help with that now by summarising facts and integrating it into pre-existing worldviews (such as a model built by your bank's researchers </news/ai-in-research-finance>).
Speaking on the M&A Science podcast <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zaq3wiQvWXM&t=1s>, Avinash Patel, a partner at M&A investment banking boutique </news/boutique-investment-banks> PJT Partners, said that the analytical part of the job doesn’t just mean adding one plus one. He asks his junior bankers a simple question: “why are you adding one and one together? And how is it helping our client to understand a problem?”
M&A careers involve long hours. Our 2026 Compensation & Lifestyle Report </banking-compensation-guide> found that M&A bankers have, for the last four years, worked 68 or so hours a week on average. That number is much, much higher than any of its fellow job categories. That requires stamina. An M&A banker </news/what-s-it-really-like-to-work-in-m-and-a-a-day-in-the-life-of-a-junior-m-and-a-banker> we spoke to a few years ago said that she was usually in the office from 9am to midnight, a 15 hour workday – implying a 75-hour work week, if she isn’t working on weekends. She probably is.
Along with good analytical skills, a strong work ethic and a good attitude are therefore essential. “A good banker needs to be committed to the job and the deals they are working on,” said John Hannon a few years ago, head of UK M&A for UBS, who also notes that a good attitude is vital. “It is essential to maintain a positive attitude as you are constantly interacting with others; a bad attitude could be detrimental to the whole team.” Hannon also says a sense of humor is important, although that probably won’t be enough on its own.
As an analyst starts to climb the ladder, their career evolves in many directions. “This is a career that celebrates achievement by changing your role,” Goldman Sachs’ head of entertainment banking, Aaron Siegel, told Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/goldman-hollywood-banker-aaron-siegel-talks-ai-anxiety-junior-bankers-2025-6> last year in June.
“As an analyst, you spend two or three years mastering modelling,” Siegel said. “As an associate, your task is to oversee the narrative of presentation materials. And once you master that, you are then moved into a new role as a VP managing projects and the day-to-day work with clients.”
Patel said that, at PJT, the difference between a VP and an analyst or associate </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> is not just executing the deal as we noted above by “adding one plus one”, but also “taking all of that execution, but putting insights, advice, and tactics on top of it."
As a senior banker, this responsibility grows beyond just the deal you are working on too - you need to have a broad view of the industry as a whole. “If a client needs to know what the industry landscape looks like, we should be able to show up and talk about who are the different players, who's up-and-coming, who's struggling, and who's valued how and why,” Patel explained. “You cannot show up and give a cookie-cutter response... Every specific situation dictates a different piece of advice, and that takes time, effort, and thinking. It’s a constant Rubik's Cube – you got a new one every few minutes to solve."
Even later in your career, your life and job slowly begin to merge into one. Managing and developing client relationships is the name of the game. Siegel, who is a managing director, noted that he goes for a run in Central Park in the morning – if he’s up early enough – and uses the chance to call and catch up with ongoing projects in Europe and Asia.
Patel explained that, even when you “don’t have relationships”, you can build them quickly. “When you're a junior banker, you're working on deals, there's going to be a counterpart at the company that you're probably all just in the mud together while the senior people are talking higher-level concepts.” All of those people on that team will end up somewhere, Patel explained. “If you just do a good job and are a good junior deal team member, you've actually slowly started building a network."

item.title: HSBC is thinking of increasing bonuses. This is who should get them
item.description:
If it likes you, HSBC does not pay you badly. Last year it paid senior bankers who were material risk takers $1.4m each </news/hsbc-is-paying-senior-bankers-who-stay-1-4m-and-senior-bankers-who-go-500k>and some were pleasantly surprised </news/hey-hsbc-s-us-bonuses-were-really-great-actually>although others quickly went on their way due to possible disappointment. </news/more-exits-from-hsbc-s-dcm-team-in-london-post-bonuses>
This year, HSBC might pay a bit more. In its first half investor presentation today, the bank said it "may consider increasing variable pay." CEO Georges Elhedery, said this consideration will occur at the end of the year.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Given that we are around five months from the end of the year, it's notable that Elhedery has flagged this potential consideration now. Ostensibly, he did so to prepare investors for a "modest" increase in HSBC's costs. Equally, though, he might be signalling to HSBC's people that they should stick around. Barclays is increasing bonuses </news/barclays-lower-salaries-higher-bonuses>, after all, and their heads might be turned.
Who should get the higher HSBC bonuses if they are forthcoming? HSBC's debt capital markets (DCM) originators have long whinged about being overlooked in favour of syndicate bankers and might benefit from more love. Bankers and traders at the London non-ring-fenced bank, who increased profits 63% year-on-year in the first half to $805m might feel entitled to something; so too might people in the US business, where profits more than doubled to over $500m. At the main Hong Kong entity, by comparison, profits were down 1.3% in the investment bank over the same period.
Revenues in HSBC's investment bank were less impressive in the first half. Globally, investment banking revenues were up less than 1% in the six month period, and sales and trading revenues were up less than 4%. Most rival banks achieved comfortable high double digit percentage increases. However, HSBC has been "simplifying" its business, closing its M&A and ECM businesses </news/hscb-closure-europe-us-job-cuts>outside of Asia and the Middle East and ejecting various members of its equities business </news/hsbc-s-pre-bonus-equities-job-cuts>, so a comparative shrinking is inevitable.
While it considers increasing bonuses, HSBC is also cutting costs. The bank said today that it now intends to increase its restructuring savings to $2bn from $1.7bn currently, and that these will be "actioned before the end of the year."
Some of the costs cut so far have come when people have left HSBC of their own accord, but Elhedery said today that the new cuts will also come from opportunities to save money. The implication is that more people may be cut before bonuses are paid. These people may be in areas like onboarding, KYC, credit workflows, contact centres, and legacy products, where HSBC is having great success in introducing AI.
The bank is not only thinking of spending more money on bonuses. It's also spending an extra $100m on branch security and other things "given the heightened risk environment."

item.title: Equity researchers are getting $800k+, finding jobs easier these days
item.description:
Bank’s equity researchers </news/research-job-investment-bank> might not be as well paid as their colleagues in investment banking </news/the-investment-banking-recruitment-process> or sales & trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank>, but it’s hardly a career in volunteering.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
A recent salary survey from recruitment firm Octavius Finance showed that UK-based long-only equity researchers can earn up to and over £600k ($806k) in total compensation, with salaries of up to £225k ($302k) and bonuses of up to and over 150% of base.
2026 has been a year of investment in long-only research after a long period of decline. Octavius Finance said that there was an “an extended period of cautious headcount management,” but now hiring was in a “rebuild” mode even though hiring remained “selective”.
It was a different story for long-short researchers. “Demand across the equity long/short space has remained resilient,” Octavius Finance said, but was focused on sector specialists. Long/short analysts, who usually work at hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>, could claim up to £200k ($267k) in salary depending on experience, with profit share related to the performance of their fund “typical”. Of course, a good enough analyst at a hedge fund becomes a portfolio manager, which unlocks a completely new tier of compensation potential.
Either way, rebuilding is a slow process. Euromoney reported <https://www.euromoney.com/article/2e56vluxaqfm2a7b8jn5s/capital-markets/is-the-brain-drain-over-new-research-shows-reversal-of-broker-juniorisation-trend/> at the end of 2024 that about 7,500 years of “net experience” had left the industry between 2018 and 2021, and only about 1,400 years of experience had returned.
This is, of course, related to the MiFID unbundling saga, which meant that banks had to charge buy-side clients separately for using their sales & trading and research services, rather than just charging them together in a bundle. Unbundling rules have since been revoked, but the damage is likely fatal to the industry.
Of course, AI is also impacting careers in research </news/ai-in-research-finance>. Specialist producers are capable of churning out reams and reams of industry-grade research for comparatively low token costs. But there is one thing that AI cannot do, and it is an extremely lucrative skill to have: “original investment thinking remains one of the clearest differentiators between candidates,” Octavius Finance said.

item.title: Morgan Stanley's head of European high yield trading disappeared from the desk
item.description:
Where is Jon Stead, the head of high yield trading at Morgan Stanley? Not, it seems, at Morgan Stanley any more.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Stead didn't respond to a request to comment. Morgan Stanley declined to comment. But multiple sources say Stead is no longer there. He is thought to be joining a hedge fund. Maybe Point72, but we have not confirmed this.
This is the second time Stead has left Morgan Stanley. He worked for the bank in London for nearly eight years after leaving the London School of Economics. He joined Citi for a brief four months and then returned to Morgan Stanley where he's been since 2021 and has been head of high yield trading since 2023.
By our reckoning Stead might be aged 35.
He is not the first Morgan Stanley credit trader to leave the business in London. There were various departures in late 2024 and 2025 amidst complaints of favouritism </news/morgan-stanley-credit-traders-leaving>. One trader who left joined hedge fund Verition but left again </news/hedge-fund-verition-s-senior-credit-traders-from-morgan-stanley-and-bof-a-have-gone> after less than a year.

item.title: DRW raised pay to £340k per head in London after hiring
item.description:
Last year was not the best of years for Don Wilson’s electronic trading firm </news/high-frequency-trading-hiring-and-pay>-cum family office, at least if its London office </news/hft-pay-london> is anything to go by. DRW </news/ex-goldman-sachs-md-that-replicated-strategies-of-trading-firms-just-joined-one>’s primary UK entity swung from a £6.2m profit in 2024 to a £3.5m operating loss in 2025. This hasn’t stopped the firm from hiring, or from compensating its traders.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Accounts for 2025, released via companies house show that ‘DRW UK Partners LLP’ increased headcount by 54 to 376 people. Headcount grew by 36 people in its technology division and 20 in trading, </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank>but DRW trimmed headcount in operations.
Compensation per head increased last year despite the operating loss. Employees earned an average of £321k in 2024 in 'wages and salaries' versus £340.9k in 2025. Total staff expenses were up £30.9m, equivalent to roughly three quarters of the additional expenses DRW UK Partners had last year. An FX swing and a VAT write-off account for the majority of the other additional expenses.
DRW UK Partners LLP provides support services to DRW, rather than acting as a separate entity, so it's not clear exactly how its trading activities performed. DRW has two other visible entities, 'DRW Global Markets Ltd' and 'DRW Investments (UK) Limited', which made a combined profit of £1.2m
Elsewhere, some of DRW's other traders have had more visible issues. The FT <https://www.ft.com/content/58558368-a938-4194-ba0d-cb10f3a0915d?syn-25a6b1a6=1> reported in June that it parted ways with its North American head of power and natural gas trading after the firm made an adjusted loss of $176m in the first quarter of 2026.

item.title: Morning Coffee: The 20 students for whom a $500k private equity job would be horribly boring. UBS's unfortunate Excel spreadsheet
item.description:
Getting a job at a top private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> firm is not easy. If you achieve one, you are supposed to say things like "it's much better being an investor than an advisor" and "secondaries are a valuable source of liquidity in a difficult market." You are not supposed to find your junior private equity job more tedious than the work you were doing as part of your university investment group.
20 undergraduate students at Indiana University face this peril. The Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/this-high-powered-real-estate-fund-is-run-by-college-students-11ad5ebb?mod=hp_lead_pos8> reports that they are part of a $12m private equity real estate fund, 'Sample Gates Management,' run by undergraduates. They screen up to 400 investments per year, but between 2023 and 2025 they only invested in 12. This summer they sold their first investment - an industrial warehouse development in Indianapolis - and made a gross profit of 65% in 16 months.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The 20 students are genuine investors and are involved in the entire process. When a potential investment passes the initial screening, they present it to a committee of 10 seasoned real estate executives. This committee rejects a third of their suggestions.
The students are also involved in fundraising. In 2022 they raised $4.2m from 46 investors.
Getting into Sample Gates Management is not easy. 278 students at Indiana University are studying real estate and would presumably all like to be investing the $12m. However, it's easier than getting into Blackstone, which is known to have an acceptance rate of 0.3% or less for its graduate programme </news/2023/07/blackstone-graduate-program>and to be a hyper competitive employer at associate level when it employs juniors from banks.
Blackstone Associates can earn $500k <https://prospectrockpartners.com/private-equity-compensation-base-salary-bonus-and-carried-interest/> according to recruitment firm Prospect Rock Partners. But one Indiana University alum who worked for Sample Gates Management says a junior job at Blackstone would be "mentally defeating" for students who have worked at the highest level of deal processes at Sample Gates. Instead of actually managing a fund and selecting investments, they will be mostly working on spreadsheets and building financial models </news/2022/06/day-in-the-life-private-equity-blackstone>as juniors at large funds.
Good luck with that. Many of the students already have jobs lined up. They might be able to teach their bosses a few things.
Separately, in this age of AI there are areas in banks that still rely upon Excel spreadsheets. Citi's wealth business was accused </news/citi-stands-accused-of-attempting-to-implement-ai-on-the-back-of-excel-spreadsheets> of attempting to implement AI on the back of spreadsheets in 2024 and now UBS has fallen foul of a secret spreadsheet in 2026.
The Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/03c413f2-6ad5-45d1-b5ac-fdb6ed8b4cff?syn-25a6b1a6=1>reports that UBS has been fined $125m for poor money laundering controls and that the Swiss bank was using a 'complex monitoring system that included an Excel spreadsheet.'
In this way, potential money launderers went unnoticed and UBS allowed tens of millions in transactions for someone close to Vladimir Putin in Russia.
UBS had similar issues with money laundering controls in 2018 and was supposed to have fixed them. The director of the US Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network described the bank as "recidivist" and said it is now facing "severe repercussions" in the large fine. Other banks with inappropriate Excel spreadsheets should take heed.
Meanwhile...
Jeff Tannenbaum took over Bank of America's EMEA corporate and investment bank last year and he's implemented a system where bad managers don't have to manage and are free to go hang out with clients. "Investment banks are notorious for promoting their best producers into leadership roles. But being a precocious dealmaker doesn’t necessarily make them a good manager." (Financial News) < https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/bank-of-america-emea-boss-tannenbaum-we-are-back-to-where-we-belong-18e921ca?mod=topic_news>
Citi hired Rohan Sen from Bank of America to cover the technology services sector. It also hired five technology bankers last month. (Reuters) <https://www.reuters.com/world/citi-hires-bank-americas-rohan-sen-lead-technology-services-banking-2026-08-03/>
The prime brokers </news/prime-broking-banks-2026>for the Situational Awareness </news/citadel-leopold-aschenbrenner-situational-awareness> fund are Goldman Sachs, Bank of America and JPMorgan. They will recall the situation with Archegos where Goldman Sachs avoided losses by exiting its positions before the rest. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2026-08-03/situational-awareness-439-return-should-have-been-a-warning?taid=6a7061f5423cf600011cdc3c&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Millennium lost 2.1% last month, seemingly on equities investments. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-03/millennium-lost-2-last-month-as-ai-trade-whipsawed-hedge-funds?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=260803&utm_campaign=author_19458291>
Palantir's revenue increased 94% in Q2 to $1.94 billion on a year-over-year basis. CEO Alex Karp said this was "otherworldly." He also said it was because customers want "AI sovereignty" and "maximal control over their operations, data, and decisions. Their competitive advantage should never become the training data for future models.” (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/business/earnings/palantir-lifts-guidance-as-revenue-nearly-doubles-f4d79fa7?mod=hp_lead_pos6>
James Dacombe is a 25-year-old entrepreneur with a $3.3bn chip business. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/7a8c03c7-1c33-4ba7-a768-a75fa1db9f36?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Anthony Jenkins, the former CEO of Barclays just secured a £40m capital injection for the technology business he launched 10 years ago. He won't say how much it's worth. He is saying: "Every bank wants to be an AI bank, but almost none can be, on a forty-year-old core." (Sky) <https://news.sky.com/story/former-barclays-chief-jenkins-raises-40m-for-tech-platform-10x-banking-13569457>
People still want to live in Dubai. Jordan Rochester, head of fixed income strategy at Mizuho in London, is the latest to go there. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-08-03/uae-jobs-mr-brexit-joins-finance-elite-moving-to-the-middle-east?taid=6a706db2fbc2220001025c31&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Banking jobs in the 1990s. “The hangover was part of the job. It was acceptable to drag your sorry ass to your desk at 7.30am and go, ‘Oh my god, that was a wild night, wasn’t it?’ and everyone else would say, ‘Yeah, it was great, wasn’t it? Corporate finance were all over the place – they were more hungover than we were. They were a shambles..." (Stylist) <https://www.stylist.co.uk/health/banker-hangover-tips-workday-2/1102066>

item.title: A US hedge fund closed its US gas trading business. Banks & hedge funds are hiring its people
item.description:
Natural gas trading can be a lucrative business. Just ask Citadel, </news/citadel-energy-trading> which the FT says made $8bn <https://www.ft.com/content/3d0842dd-a8f4-435d-b888-5587b4b9eeda?syn-25a6b1a6=1> in profits trading it when the Ukraine war broke out in 2022. $2bn of that was made by a single trader (Chris Foster), who can be seen here wearing pink socks. <https://www.mansfield.ox.ac.uk/for-mansfield-forever/meet-our-lead-benefactor/>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Not all natural gas trading teams make money, though. In January, Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-16/hedge-fund-roscommon-analytics-shutters-us-gas-desk>reported that US hedge fund Roscommon Analytics had lost money and was closing its US gas desk. Roscommon people have been leaving ever since. They have also been turning up elsewhere.
We count at least 11 traders who've left Roscommon Analytics in 2026. Seven of them have new roles. It's not clear whether they all come from Roscommon's natural gas desk.
Those seven include James Degelia, Roscommon's chief risk officer for the US, who just joined Balyasny, and Samantha Philipp West, who left in January but who just joined Citi as a VP power trader. In April, Paul Matasso joined Marathon Petroleum Corporation as head of natural gas trading; Daniel Hassouni joined Saracen Energy; and Rishi Khullar joined Trafigura. Logan Graham joined Castleton Commodities as a power strategist in January. Adam O'Shay joined BofA as a director of North East power trading in February. And Michael Ciano, whose arrival from Hartree in March 2025 contributed to Roscommon's natural gas buildout, but who moved to the ever-acquisitive SquarePoint </news/hedge-fund-squarepoint-is-quietly-ramping-up-its-commodities-trading-business>in February.
If you want to participate in the Roscommon Analytics hiring party, it's not too late. Various members of the team have indicated on LinkedIn that their time at the fund has come to an end but that something completely new has yet to begin. Many are based in Houston. They include: Ross Sclafani (a power trader); Suresh Dongre (the chief information officer), William Smith (a London-based power and gas data architect); and Michael Britt (a former MD on the treasury team).
Roscommon Analytics didn't comment for this article. Speaking to Bloomberg in January, its CEO Kevin Kelly said the firm was well capitalized and "operating in an orderly manner." Its most recently filed regulatory ADV form says it has 95 employees of whom 45 are investment staff. The fund's own site says it has offices in Houston and New York City. It currently has 31 people registered on LinkedIn, versus over twice that number a year ago.
